1.open: Think of a time you were new somewhere, like a new school, job or town. What helped you feel like you belonged?
questions: Peter writes to "exiles" scattered across several regions (v. 1). Have you ever felt like an outsider, at work, in your family or among friends? What was that like?
Verse 3 says God "has given us new birth into a living hope." What does hope look like in ordinary life for you right now, and where is it hard to find?
Peter describes an inheritance that is "imperishable, undefiled, and unfading" (v. 4). Why would people who were struggling need to hear that? What do we tend to count on that can spoil or fade?

Verses 6 and 7 compare trials to fire that tests gold, so that "the proven character of your faith" may come to light. How do you hear that when you are in a hard season? Is it comforting, difficult, or both?

In verse 8 Peter says, "Though you have not seen Him, you love Him." Faith can feel quiet or uncertain at times. What is it like for you to trust someone you cannot see, and where do you honestly stand today?
Peter says, "be holy in all you do" (v. 15). What do you picture when you hear the word holy? How does it change things to know it means being set apart for God, not being perfect?
Peter says we were redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ," not with "silver or gold" (vv. 18, 19). What does it mean to you that you were bought back at such a cost, and not by your own effort?
Verse 22 urges, "love one another deeply, from a pure heart." What does that kind of love look like in a small group like ours, and what makes it hard?
1.life: Peter says the believers' hope is safe even when life is not. This week, name one thing you have been leaning on that could be lost, and tell God you are placing your hope in Jesus instead. Then do one practical act of love for someone in your group.
1.prayer: Thank God for "a living hope" and for an inheritance that cannot fade. Ask him to steady anyone in the group who feels like an outsider or is going through a trial right now.
1.tip: Verse 2 raises the old question of what "foreknowledge" means, and Christians differ: some think God chose people by his own decision ahead of time, others that he chose knowing who would come to trust him. Say that plainly in one line, then bring the group back to Peter's point, which is comfort for people who feel scattered and unsure. Also go gently with verses 6 and 7, since someone may be in real pain and not need a lesson about trials.

2.open: When you were a kid, what was a place or group where you really felt you belonged?
questions: Peter says to rid ourselves of "malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander" (v. 1). Which of these sneaks into everyday life most easily, and what does it do to relationships?
Peter pictures believers as newborns who "crave pure spiritual milk" (v. 2). What do you find yourself hungry for these days, and how does that compare with hunger for God?
Jesus is called "the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight" (v. 4). What does it mean to you that the one God chose was first rejected?
Peter says "you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house" (v. 5). Why might it matter that we are built together and not as separate stones?

Verse 9 calls believers "a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation." Christians disagree about what a priesthood of all believers means for ordained clergy. Whatever your tradition, what do you think it means that every believer has direct access to God?
Verse 10 says "once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy." Where have you seen mercy change someone's story, yours or another person's?

Peter tells believers to live so that others "may see your good deeds and glorify God" (v. 12), even when they are slandered. What does answering suspicion with good deeds look like where you live and work?

Verse 23 says Jesus "did not retaliate" but "entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly." If you are honest, what makes it hard to let go of a wrong done to you, and what might trusting God with it look like?
2.life: Think of one person who has treated you unfairly or who may misjudge you. This week, do one quiet, good thing for them or about them, and give the hurt to God in prayer.
2.prayer: Thank God that you are now "the people of God" and have received mercy. Ask for help to answer unfair treatment as Jesus did, and pray for the group to be built together.
2.tip: Verses 18 to 20 speak to slaves and can be misused to excuse abuse or to tell suffering people to stay silent. Say plainly that Peter is describing real people in a harsh system and pointing to Christ's example, not blessing cruelty. Keep the focus on verses 21 to 25 and on how Jesus carried injustice, and be careful with anyone in the group who may be in a painful situation now.

3.open: Think of someone whose way of living made you curious about what they believed. What did you notice about them?
questions: Peter writes to Christian wives whose husbands do not share their faith, and says they may be "won over without words by the behavior of their wives" (v. 1). Why can a quiet life sometimes say more than an argument?
Peter says real beauty is "the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God's sight" (v. 4). What does our culture say makes a person valuable, and how does this differ?

Christians read verses 1 to 6 differently. Some see a pattern for marriage in every age, others see guidance for Christian wives in a risky setting in the first century. Why might both groups point to verse 7 and its picture of husband and wife as "fellow heirs"?
Verse 9 says, "Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing." Think of a time someone wronged you. What makes blessing them so hard, and what might it look like in practice?
Peter says that even if we suffer for doing right, "you are blessed" (v. 14). What do you make of that, and how does it sit with your own experience of hard times?

Verse 15 says, "Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you." If a friend asked why you hope, what would you honestly say? It is fine to say you are not sure.
Peter adds, "But respond with gentleness and respect" (v. 15). Why do you think how we answer matters as much as what we say?
Verse 18 says Christ suffered "the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." How does knowing Jesus went through unfair suffering change the way you think about your own?
3.life: This week, pick one person who is hard to get along with. Each time they annoy or hurt you, respond with a kind word or a quiet prayer for them instead of getting even.
3.prayer: Ask God for a gentle and steady spirit when people are unkind. Pray for anyone in the group who is facing pressure or mistreatment, and for hope that others can see.
3.tip: Verses 1 to 6 can be painful, and verses 19 to 21 can pull the whole evening into debate. Say early that Christians disagree on both, and that submission never means staying in danger or accepting abuse. Anyone being harmed should seek safety and help. Then steer back to verses 8 to 18, where the chapter's main point is found.

4.open: Think of a time you were the only one in a group who did something differently, like skipping dessert, leaving early or cheering for the other team. How did it feel?
questions: Peter says you "have spent enough time in the past" living the old way (v. 3). What does it look like in everyday life to leave an old habit or crowd behind, and what makes it hard?

Verse 4 says old friends "consider it strange of you not to plunge with them" and "heap abuse on you." Why do you think people react that way when someone changes? How could we respond with kindness rather than pride?

Verse 6 is hard to pin down, and Christians read it in different ways. A common reading is that believers who have since died did hear the good news while alive. What hope does the passage give us even when some things are unclear?

Peter says, "love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins" (v. 8). What is the difference between love that covers over a fault and love that ignores a problem? Where have you been on the receiving end of that kind of love?
Verse 9 says to "show hospitality to one another without complaining." What makes hospitality tiring, and what has made it a joy when someone has done it for you?

Verse 10 calls us "good stewards of the manifold grace of God" who use "whatever gift" we have "to serve one another." What is one thing you are able to do that could help someone in this group, even if it feels small?

Peter writes, "do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you" (v. 12). Has a hard season ever caught you off guard? What did it do to your picture of God, and what, if anything, are you still wrestling with?
Verse 19 closes with "entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good." What would it look like for you to do that this week in a situation that is weighing on you?
4.life: Pick one person who is going through something hard, or one small way to serve your church or neighbors. Do it this week without needing anyone to notice, and pray as you do it that God would supply the strength (v. 11).
4.prayer: Thank God that he is a "faithful Creator" who can be trusted with our hardest days. Ask him to help each person in the group to love deeply, serve with the strength he gives, and trust him with whatever they are carrying right now.
4.tip: Verses 12 to 16 can lead people to compare hardships or to feel that their own struggles are too small, or too big, to share. Remind the group that Peter is speaking about being shamed for Jesus, which is different from the ordinary troubles we bring on ourselves (v. 15), and that every kind of hurt is welcome here. Also, do not try to settle verse 6 in the meeting. Say once that Christians read it differently and move on.

5.open: Who is someone who looked out for you when you were younger, and what did they do that you still remember?
questions: Peter calls himself "a fellow elder" before he gives any instructions (v. 1). How does it change the way you hear advice when the person giving it stands beside you instead of above you?
Peter asks leaders to watch over people "not out of compulsion, but willingly" (v. 2). What does it look like to serve out of eagerness rather than duty, at church, at home or at work?
He warns against "lording it over those entrusted to you" and asks for "examples to the flock" (v. 3). Think of a leader who led by example. What made you trust them?
Verse 5 says, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." What is the difference between real humility and putting yourself down?

Verse 7 says, "Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you." What makes it hard to actually let go of a worry, even when we believe this? Be as honest as you like, including if it feels hard to believe.

Peter says to be "sober-minded and alert" because the adversary "prowls around like a roaring lion" (v. 8). What pressures or fears can pull a person away from trusting God, and how can we help each other stay steady?
Verse 9 reminds them that "your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering." How does it help to know you are not the only one struggling?

In verse 10 God promises that after "a little while" of suffering He will "restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you." Which of those four words do you most need to hear right now, and why?
5.life: Each day this week, name one specific worry out loud to God, then say verse 7 back to him: he cares for you. If it comes back, hand it over again. Also pick one person to encourage, since Peter reminds us we are not alone.
5.prayer: Thank God that he cares for you and is the "God of all grace." Ask him to help you hand over specific worries, and pray for the leaders of your church to serve gently and willingly.
5.tip: Verses 8 and 9 can lead to long talk about the devil or to fear. Keep the group on Peter's point: stay clear-headed, hold on, and remember you are not alone. Also, verse 7 can sound too easy to someone in real distress, so make room for people to say that letting go is hard, and avoid quick fixes.
